ideas.title: Fault Line
ideas.concept: Players are rival geological survey consortiums racing to stake claims on a growing continental plate. Every tile you lock into the shared fault grid adds pressure to the region around it, and when pressure crosses the threshold the whole fault chain violently 'settles' — locking in points but resetting the pressure race. Every placement is a bet on how close you can push a fault line before someone else claims the release.
ideas.differentiation: An original tile-laying/area-control game built around a physical peg-stacking pressure-cascade resolution: pressure accumulates visibly on pegs across a contiguous chain of tiles, and crossing a fixed threshold triggers a chain-wide 'quake' that flips tiles and pays out points. Searched 'board game tectonic plate tile pressure cascade chain reaction area control' (top hits: educational Plate Tectonics classroom games, and Plate Smash, whose mechanic is players physically pulling plates apart/together to attack, not a threshold-triggered pressure-cascade tile flip) and 'board game chain reaction tile flip threshold scoring' — no existing shipped product combines contiguous-chain pressure summing with a peg-stack visual threshold trigger.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players. Setup: assemble the hex frame board (61 hex sockets arranged in 5 concentric rings around a center hex). Each player takes 20 Plate tiles in their color (each embossed with a stress value of 1, 2, or 3, roughly 7/7/6 split) and a score marker on the perimeter track at 0. Place the neutral center hex tile (stress 0) into the frame to start. On your turn: (1) Place one of your Plate tiles into any empty hex socket orthogonally adjacent to at least one already-placed tile. (2) Add pressure pegs onto that tile's peg-hole equal to its stress value, then add pressure pegs equal to that same value onto every tile directly adjacent to it that is already part of the same contiguous placed-tile chain. (3) Sum all pressure pegs currently on every tile in that fault chain. If the sum is 7 or more, trigger a Quake: every tile in the chain flips to its reverse 'settled' face, you score 1 point per tile flipped, all pressure pegs on those tiles return to the supply, and settled tiles can never receive pressure again (they still count for adjacency/area purposes). If the sum is below 7, nothing else happens and play passes left. The game ends when no empty socket has a legal placement or any player runs out of Plate tiles. Final scoring: each player adds 1 bonus point per settled tile of their color in the single largest contiguous group of same-color settled tiles on the board. Highest total score wins; ties go to the player with the most unsettled tiles remaining in hand.
ideas.components: 1 hex frame board printed in 3 bolt-together 120-degree wedge segments (PLA, ~300mm assembled diameter, 61 recessed hex sockets 32mm flat-to-flat); 80 Plate tiles (20 x 4 colors, hex, 30mm flat-to-flat x 5mm thick, double-sided — front embossed with stress value 1-3, back embossed with a settled fault-crack texture); 1 center neutral hex tile (stress 0); 140 pressure peg tokens (cylindrical, 6mm dia x 5mm tall, gray PLA, friction-fit, stackable); 1 perimeter score track ring (0-60 track) with 4 slide-fit score markers; box.
ideas.demand_case: Area-control tile-laying is one of BGG's largest mechanism categories, with comparable hits like Kingdomino and Suburbia each holding tens of thousands of owners, and chain-reaction resolution is the signature hook of well-established abstract games like Ingenious and Blokus. Target audience: family-to-mid-weight strategy gamers, ages 10+, who like Kingdomino/Blokus-style tile games with more tension.
ideas.fun_case: Every placement is a two-sided bet — push the chain closer to a quake to bank guaranteed points now, or hold back so a rival's placement doesn't trigger a payout you don't control — the same risk-timing tension that makes Ingenious's chain-scoring and push-your-luck games compelling. ~30-45 min playtime fits family/gateway weight; the physical peg-stacking gives tactile feedback a numeric tracker can't replicate.
ideas.producibility_notes: 6 distinct part types. Frame wedges bolt together via 3 printed snap-lugs (0.3mm clearance) — a single static assembly step at setup, not a repeated per-turn joint. Pressure pegs are simple friction-fit cylinders into 6.2mm holes (0.2mm clearance) repeated ~140 times using one validated peg/hole geometry, so risk doesn't compound with count. No features under 1mm. No electronics or springs.
ideas.prompt: A tabletop product photo of the board game 'Fault Line': a circular hexagonal game board about 30cm across made of matte dark-gray 3D-printed plastic, divided into dozens of small hexagon sockets, with colorful hex tiles (red, blue, yellow, green) plugged into a spiral pattern radiating from the center, small gray cylindrical peg tokens stacked in clusters on some tiles showing 'pressure,' a thin printed scoring ring wrapping the board's outer edge with four colored slider markers, all sitting on a wood table next to a sturdy cardboard game box printed with a stylized cracked-earth tectonic-fault graphic in orange and charcoal, studio lighting, isometric product-photography angle.

ideas.title: Orbital Drift
ideas.concept: A three-ring turntable is the whole game board, and it physically rotates every turn — the satellites you and your rivals placed last round are never where you left them. You're racing to line up your own colored satellites into straight radial constellations before the spin scrambles your plans, turning simple placement into a constantly shifting spatial puzzle.
ideas.differentiation: The nearest comparable product, GPS (a spinner-based satellite-launch board game), uses only a single abstract spinner to randomly determine one launch slot per turn and never physically moves already-placed pieces. Orbital Drift's core mechanism is different: the entire multi-ring board physically rotates one notch every turn, continuously reshuffling the spatial relationship between previously placed tokens, turning alignment into an ongoing puzzle rather than a one-shot placement lottery. Searched 'board game rotating turntable orbit ring satellite placement dexterity space game' and 'rotating board game satellite constellation alignment' — found GPS (single spinner, no board rotation) and generic orbital-themed strategy titles (Orbital, Orbital Velocity, Junk Orbit) with no physical rotation mechanic; no existing product combines a physically rotating multi-ring board with post-rotation radial alignment scoring.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players. Setup: assemble the turntable (inner ring 6 pegs, middle ring 9 pegs, outer ring 12 pegs, mounted on a center pivot so the whole assembly rotates freely) with the fixed launch marker arrow pointing at peg 0 on each ring. Each player takes 6 satellite cone tokens in their color. On your turn: (1) Roll both dice. Die A (1-2=inner, 3-4=middle, 5-6=outer) picks the ring. Die B (1-6) counts empty pegs clockwise from the launch marker on that ring; place a satellite on the first empty peg reached counting that many empty pegs (if fewer empty pegs remain, place on the last empty one). (2) Rotate the entire turntable clockwise exactly one peg-position. (3) Check alignment: look along the 12 fixed radial sighting lines printed on the base mat beneath the turntable — if two or more of your own satellites (any ring) now sit on the same radial line, score fuel-cell chips: 2 for a 2-satellite line, 5 for a 3-satellite line (flip a flag on scored satellites so they don't rescore the same alignment). Play passes left. The game ends when all 27 pegs are filled. Most fuel-cell chips wins; ties broken by most satellites on the outer ring.
ideas.components: 1 turntable assembly — 3 concentric printed rings (80mm/140mm/200mm diameter) fixed together by 3 radial spokes into one rigid rotating disc, mounted on a center pivot pin + bushing on a fixed base plate (6mm pin, 0.3mm clearance), 27 peg holes total; 24 satellite cone tokens (6 per color x 4 colors, 15mm tall, each with a small flip-flag for marking 'scored'); 1 fixed base mat printed with 12 radial sighting lines; 2 dice (d6); 60 fuel-cell chips (hex, engraved '2' or '5'); box.
ideas.demand_case: Dexterity/spatial-rotation mechanics are an established BGG mechanism category with strong sellers (Pitchcar, Junk Art, Ice Cool all hold tens of thousands of owners), and space/orbital theming has proven family appeal via games like GPS. Target audience: family game night, ages 8+, players who enjoy a physical, tactile randomizer-driven game with light spatial strategy.
ideas.fun_case: Because your own past placements keep moving out from under you, every turn forces re-evaluation of whether your constellation is still forming or was just ruined by the last rotation — the same live-board-state tension that makes Blokus and Ice Cool replayable despite simple rules. ~20-30 min playtime and one-glance rules fit the family audience; the physically rotating board is the table-presence hook distinguishing it from GPS's single abstract spinner.
ideas.producibility_notes: Riskiest joint is the center pivot bearing — a 6mm pin with a printed bushing sleeve at 0.3mm clearance, which should be printed and hand-tested for smooth rotation before locking the STL; it's a known joint type (peg-in-sleeve rotation) with rotation fully player-controlled, not a novel unpredictable physics-dependent mechanism. 27 peg holes at 5mm/0.2mm clearance (repeated, low risk, one validated geometry). No features under 1mm.
ideas.prompt: A tabletop product photo of the board game 'Orbital Drift': a round three-tiered rotating turntable game board about 20cm across, made of glossy dark-navy 3D-printed plastic with metallic silver ring accents, small colorful cone-shaped satellite tokens (red, blue, yellow, green) dotted around its concentric rings, sitting on a square base mat printed with thin white radiating sightlines like a star chart, two dice beside it, next to a sleek black-and-silver cardboard game box with a starfield and orbiting-planet graphic, dramatic overhead studio lighting emphasizing the rings, isometric product-photography angle.

ideas.title: Dune Runner
ideas.concept: You're a caravan trader racing rivals between oasis trading posts, but a slotted disc laid over the desert grid physically blocks a shifting set of dunes each round — and unlike a random card draw, you can see exactly which hexes go dark next because the disc's rotation pattern is fixed and readable. The tension is entirely route-planning: commit to a path before the sand closes it.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: the shifting-terrain-hazard blocking movement popularized by Forbidden Desert (cooperative survival, hazard driven by random card draws that add persistent sand-counter stacks to individual tiles). Rule-level change: Dune Runner replaces that with a physical rotating windowed overlay disc whose 12-notch rotation pattern is fixed and fully visible/plannable in advance (no randomness in which hexes block next), and restructures the game from cooperative survival into a competitive pickup-and-deliver trading race with no persistent per-tile counters. Searched 'board game rotating sandstorm disc overlay path blocking desert caravan' and 'physical rotating overlay disc board game hazard mechanism' — found only Forbidden Desert (card-driven, cooperative, counter-based) and Through the Desert (unrelated route-scoring abstract); no existing product uses a deterministic rotating windowed overlay disc for competitive route-blocking.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players. Setup: place the fixed 6x6 desert hex tray on the table with tiles pre-set per the included layout (dune, oasis, trading-post hexes). Lay the sandstorm disc (a circular overlay, roughly 2/3 solid and 1/3 cut-out window) centered on top with its index tab at position 0. Each player places their camel pawn on their assigned home trading post and takes 5 water tokens and an empty 3-slot goods rack. On your turn: (1) If you are the storm caller this round (role rotates left each round), rotate the sandstorm disc clockwise exactly one notch (12 notches total) before anyone moves — hexes under the disc's solid area are blocked this round; hexes under the window are open. (2) Move your camel up to 3 hexes through open, orthogonally-connected hexes, paying 1 water token per desert hex entered (oasis hexes cost 0 and refill you to 5 water); if you hit 0 water outside an oasis, you're stranded and skip your next full turn. (3) If you end movement on an unclaimed goods hex, take 1 goods chip if your rack has space. If you end on a trading-post hex matching a goods chip in your rack, sell it for coin tokens equal to its printed value, discarding the chip. First player to bank 15 coins wins immediately; if the goods supply runs out first, whoever has the most coins wins.
ideas.components: 1 desert tray board (printed, 6x6 recessed hex grid, ~250mm square, sand-tan PLA); 36 terrain hex tiles (20 dune, 8 oasis, 8 trading-post, 35mm flat-to-flat, snap into tray recesses); 1 sandstorm disc overlay (~260mm diameter, translucent amber PLA, cut window covering 1/3 of area, 12 rim notches, center pivot post); 4 camel pawns (25mm tall); 20 water tokens; 24 goods chips (4 colors x 6, engraved value 1-3); 60 coin tokens (denominations 1/5); 4 goods racks (3-slot trays); box.
ideas.demand_case: Pickup-and-deliver trading is an established BGG mechanism category with proven sellers (Merchants & Marauders, Ticket to Ride's route-tension cousins), and shifting-hazard-blocks-your-route is the signature hook of Forbidden Desert, a top-selling cooperative title with a large family/casual fanbase. Target audience: family/gateway strategy players, ages 10+, wanting a competitive trading race with a tactile shifting-hazard mechanism.
ideas.fun_case: The core tension each turn is route commitment under a visible but ticking clock — the storm disc's rotation pattern is knowable in advance, so the puzzle is reading 2-3 turns ahead and racing rivals to the last safe window, the same 'plan around a known-but-relentless hazard' appeal that makes Forbidden Desert replayable. ~30-40 min playtime and simple movement rules keep it accessible despite the added planning depth from a competitive structure.
ideas.producibility_notes: 5 part types. The disc overlay rotates on a center pivot post (peg + washer, 0.3mm clearance, single joint, purely geometric/visual blocking, not physics-dependent). No features under 1mm. Tile recesses in the tray need a consistent 0.2mm oversize for reliable snap-fit across 36 repeated sockets — one validated tolerance, repeated, low risk.
ideas.prompt: A tabletop product photo of the board game 'Dune Runner': a square sand-tan 3D-printed game tray divided into a 6x6 grid of hexagon terrain tiles in warm ochre and gold tones (desert dunes, blue-green oasis palms, striped trading-post tents), with a translucent amber rotating disc overlaid on top showing a cut-out window revealing some hexes while shading others darker, four small camel-shaped pawns in red, blue, yellow, and green standing on the board, tiny colored goods chips and coin tokens scattered nearby, beside a sturdy cardboard game box illustrated with a caravan silhouette crossing dunes under an orange sunset, warm studio lighting, isometric product-photography angle.

ideas.title: Cascade Works
ideas.concept: Everyone secretly and simultaneously plugs pipe segments into a shared vertical tower over several rounds, racing to claim the best sockets before rivals do — then you drop marbles from the top and watch, for real, whose plumbing actually works. It's part spatial drafting, part kinetic marble run, and the tower's final shape is different every game.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: Pipe Work's flat 2D tile-laying with pipe-shaped tiles scored by connection length between fixed tokens, no gravity flow involved. Rule-level change: Cascade Works rebuilds this as an upright 3D lattice tower with printed snap-fit pipe segments, resolved by physically dropping marbles that gravity-flow through the connected structure, plus a simultaneous secret-placement socket-claiming phase Pipe Work doesn't have. Searched 'board game simultaneous pipe tile placement marble routing race' and 'vertical 3D pipe tower marble drop board game' — found Pipe Work/Pipe Work Duo (flat, no gravity/marbles) and GraviTrax (open-ended marble-run building toy, not a scored competitive board game); no existing product combines simultaneous secret pipe-socket drafting with a competitive marble-drop scoring resolution.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players. Setup: assemble the vertical lattice tower (5 columns x 6 rows of open sockets, ~300mm tall) with 3 color-coded source openings at the top and 3 color-coded collection cups at the bottom (scrambled so a cup's color isn't necessarily under its matching source). Each player takes 10 pipe tiles in their color (mixed straight/elbow/T-junction) and a privacy screen. Play proceeds over 6 building rounds: each round, every player secretly selects one pipe tile and, behind their screen, targets an empty socket; all reveal simultaneously. If multiple players targeted the same socket, whoever rolls higher on the priority die claims it (others keep their tile for a later round); non-conflicting placements snap in immediately. After 6 rounds, run the Drop Phase: drop one marble into each of the 3 source openings and observe it flow through the connected pipes to a cup (or fall off the board, scoring nobody). For every marble that lands in a cup, every player whose colored pipe tile the marble passed through flips a flag on that tile and scores 1 point per flagged tile of their own after all 3 marbles are dropped; whoever placed the tile the marble rests in gets a 3-point bonus. Highest total score wins.
ideas.components: 1 vertical lattice tower frame (printed in 2 bolt-together halves, ~300x180x40mm, 30 open sockets in a 5x6 grid, 3 top funnels, 3 bottom color-coded cups); 40 pipe segment tiles (10 per player color: 4 straight, 3 elbow, 3 T-junction, snap-fit pegs, each with a small pivoting flag marker); 4 privacy screens; 3 marbles (16mm); 1 priority die (d6); box.
ideas.demand_case: Marble-run/kinetic-resolution games have a dedicated enthusiast following (GraviTrax has sold widely as a build-your-own marble-run system), while simultaneous secret-placement drafting is proven by games like Bohnanza and 7 Wonders' passing mechanic. Target audience: family/hobbyist crossover, ages 8+, players who enjoy a tactile 'watch it actually work' payoff on top of a planning phase.
ideas.fun_case: The two-phase structure creates a distinct decision each round — fight for a contested socket now, or bank a safe placement — followed by a genuinely unpredictable physical payoff when marbles drop, the same 'plan then watch it play out' satisfaction driving GraviTrax's popularity, compressed into a competitive 30-40 minute session. This differs materially from Pipe Work's flat scored-connection-length puzzle by resolving with an actual gravity-driven marble flow through a 3D structure.
ideas.producibility_notes: 3 part types (tower halves, pipe tiles, screens) plus dice/marbles. The tower's 2-piece bolt joint is a single static assembly (printed alignment lugs, 0.3mm clearance) done once at setup. Pipe tile snap-pegs use one validated peg/socket geometry (5mm peg, 0.2mm clearance) repeated across 40 tiles and 30 sockets — repeated but uniform, so risk doesn't compound. The one item requiring physical validation before locking the STL is marble-flow clearance at pipe-to-pipe seams (internal channel diameter must exceed 16mm marble diameter by at least 3mm throughout, including elbow/T junctions) — a dimensional/clearance check, not an unpredictable mechanism, verifiable with one printed sample set and test-drops before full production.
ideas.prompt: A tabletop product photo of the board game 'Cascade Works': a tall upright rectangular lattice tower about 30cm high made of white 3D-printed plastic with a visible grid of open square sockets, colorful pipe-segment tiles (red, blue, yellow) plugged into some sockets forming a winding path from three funnel openings at the top down to three labeled cups at the bottom, a few small steel marbles resting in the cups, small fold-out privacy screens and a die beside the tower, next to a tall narrow cardboard game box illustrated with a stylized blueprint/pipe-diagram graphic in blue and white, bright clean studio lighting, isometric product-photography angle.

ideas.title: Warren
ideas.concept: You're a rabbit clan digging tunnels out from the warren hub toward scattered carrot patches, snapping peg-connected tunnel segments together as you draw them blind from a hand-cranked dispenser — but a fox prowling the outer ring can collapse any tunnel that isn't safely connected home yet. It's build-and-connect network racing with a predator clock ticking over your shoulder.
ideas.differentiation: An original network-building race combining a hand-cranked drum dispenser (a printable substitute for a shuffled bag/deck) with a predator pawn that removes unconnected tiles it radially aligns with, forcing players to prioritize completing chains over greedy expansion. Searched 'board game rabbit burrow tunnel modular peg connector snap tile area control' and 'predator pawn removes unconnected tiles network building race game' — found themed rabbit games (Bunny Boom, Bunny Burrows, Down the Rabbit Hole) that are card-based or path-blocking puzzles with no tile-removal predator-alignment mechanic and no peg-connector tunnel network; no existing product combines these specific mechanisms.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players. Setup: place the central Hub hex in the middle of the table; scatter the 8 Carrot Patch tokens at their fixed marked outer positions on the play mat. Load all 60 tunnel tile chips face-down into the rotating drum dispenser. Place the Fox pawn on position 0 of the 24-space circular track. On your turn: (1) Crank the dispenser once to reveal one random neutral tunnel tile (straight, turn, or T-junction). (2) Place it into any empty hex position adjacent to your existing connected-to-hub network (or adjacent to the Hub if it's your first tile), snapping its peg connectors to open neighbors; mark it with a flag in your color. If it can't legally connect, discard it face-down and your turn ends with no placement. (3) Roll the d6 and advance the Fox pawn that many spaces around the track. If the Fox's new position lines up radially (per printed sightlines on the mat) with any tunnel tile not yet part of an unbroken path back to the Hub, that tile is removed from the board. The game ends when all 8 Carrot Patches are connected to the Hub, or the Fox completes 3 full laps (72 total movement), whichever comes first. Scoring: 2 points per Carrot Patch connected through a path where the majority of tiles are your flag color (ties get 1 point each), plus 1 point per tunnel tile still on the board bearing your flag. Highest score wins.
ideas.components: 1 Hub hex piece (60mm, 6 edge peg-sockets); 60 tunnel tile chips (hex, 30mm flat-to-flat, 3 shapes ~20 each, neutral tan, snap peg-and-socket connectors); 8 Carrot Patch tokens; 1 rotating drum dispenser (printed cylinder ~120mm tall with an internal spiral baffle and a single dispensing slot, hand-cranked, holds all 60 shuffled chips); 1 Fox pawn; 1 circular 24-space track ring surrounding the play mat; color-flag markers (snap-on, 4 colors); 1 play mat printed with radial sightlines and the 8 fixed patch positions; 1 d6; box.
ideas.demand_case: Network-building tile-connection games are a proven BGG category (Isle of Skye and Suburbia rank among the most-owned tile-laying titles), and animal-tunnel/burrow theming has documented recent family appeal (multiple active burrow-themed titles like Bunny Boom and Bunny Burrows). Target audience: family game night, ages 8+, players who like network/route-building with a light push-your-luck threat clock.
ideas.fun_case: The core tension is spatial commitment under threat — every tile placed is exposed to the Fox until part of an unbroken chain home, so players weigh building toward the nearest patch fast against shoring up their existing network, a risk-versus-tempo decision similar to what makes Isle of Skye's route-building and Forbidden Island's rising clock replayable. ~30-40 min playtime and a simple three-tile-shape vocabulary keep rules accessible to the family audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: 5 part types. The rotating drum dispenser is the standout custom mechanism (a hand-cranked spiral-baffle single-item feeder, a known category similar to candy/gumball dispensers, not a novel unvalidated joint); it should be print-and-test validated to confirm the baffle reliably dispenses exactly one chip per crank (spec 4mm chips with a 4.5mm internal channel, 0.5mm clearance). Tunnel tile peg/socket connectors reuse one validated geometry across 60 tiles and 6 Hub sockets (5mm peg, 0.2mm clearance) — repeated but uniform.
ideas.prompt: A tabletop product photo of the board game 'Warren': a play mat showing a circular burrow layout with a central hexagonal hub piece in warm brown 3D-printed plastic, dozens of small tan hexagonal tunnel tiles snapped together in branching paths radiating outward toward tiny orange carrot-shaped tokens, a small fox-shaped pawn on an outer circular track ring, a whimsical cylindrical hand-crank dispenser standing beside the mat with tunnel tile chips visible through a small window, next to a cardboard game box illustrated with a cutaway rabbit warren scene in earthy greens and browns, warm cozy studio lighting, isometric product-photography angle.

ideas.title: Stratum
ideas.concept: You're a geological surveyor drafting mineral-strata discs round after round, passing your leftover picks to your neighbor the way sushi gets passed at the table — except what you keep stacks permanently, in order, into your personal core-sample rack, and only the exact sequence you built can match the target pattern for bonus points. It's drafting with a spatial, order-locked twist.
ideas.differentiation: An original set-collection drafting game whose defining rule is that picks lock permanently into positional slots (an order-locked core-sample rack) rather than a free-form hand or tableau, combined with a shared randomly-revealed target sequence for bonus scoring. Searched 'board game drilling core sample stacking layered stratum mining game' and 'order-locked drafting rack positional slot scoring board game' — found Drillers (hex-based mech-exploration deck-builder, unrelated mechanic) and generic mining strategy titles; no existing product combines pass-the-tray drafting with a fixed-order, un-reorderable personal rack.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players. Setup: fill the hopper canister with all 60 strata discs (7 each of 8 rock-type colors, plus 4 rare black fossil discs). Reveal 1 random Target Pattern tile showing a 3-color sequence. Each player takes an empty 10-slot core rack (numbered slots 1-10, bottom to top). Played over 2 rounds. At the start of each round, every player draws (blind, by hand, from the hopper) a 5-disc hand-tray. Then, 5 times in a row: all players simultaneously choose 1 disc from their current tray to slot into the next open (lowest-numbered empty) slot of their core rack, then pass their remaining tray to the player on their left and pick again from the tray just received; repeat until trays are empty (5 picks per round, 2 rounds = 10 picks total, filling the 10-slot rack). End-game scoring: +3 points per fossil disc in your rack; +4 points for every complete group of 3 same-color discs anywhere in your rack (a disc counts toward only one group); +6 bonus points if slots 1-2-3 (bottom to top) exactly match the Target Pattern tile's sequence in order. Highest total wins; ties broken by most fossil discs.
ideas.components: 1 hopper canister (printed cylinder with a snap-on friction-fit lid, ~150mm tall, holds 60 discs, side dispensing slot for blind hand-draw); 60 strata discs (8 colors x 7 = 56, plus 4 black fossil discs, 25mm diameter x 5mm thick, embossed rock-texture pattern per color); 4 hand-trays (5-slot small rectangular trays, for passing); 4 core racks (10-slot vertical open-front slotted stands, ~150mm tall, keeping filled slots visible and order-locked); 8 Target Pattern tiles (double-sided, various 3-color sequences); box.
ideas.demand_case: Set-collection drafting with pass-the-hand mechanics is a large, proven BGG category — Sushi Go has over 51,000 BGG ratings and ranks in the top 1,000 games on the site, validating strong demand for exactly this draft-keep-one-pass-the-rest structure. Target audience: family/gateway gamers, ages 8+, who enjoy quick drafting games like Sushi Go or 7 Wonders' passing phase.
ideas.fun_case: The order-locked rack (no rearranging past picks) creates real tension on every pick — take the fossil disc now for guaranteed points, or hold out for the color needed to complete a set of 3 — mirroring the greedy-pick-vs-set-completion push that makes Sushi Go's scoring categories compelling round after round. ~20-25 min playtime and a simple pick-and-pass loop fit the family audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: 4 part types. The hopper canister uses a separate snap-on lid with a friction-fit rim (0.3mm clearance) rather than a living hinge, avoiding repeated-flex fatigue. Hand-trays and core racks are simple open-slot geometry with no joints, just pocket dimensions (26mm slot width for a 25mm disc, 0.5mm side clearance) — low risk. No features under 1mm. No electronics.
ideas.prompt: A tabletop product photo of the board game 'Stratum': four tall vertical slotted core-sample racks made of clear-frosted 3D-printed plastic, each holding a stack of colorful round mineral discs (amber, rust-red, slate-gray, deep green, plus a few glossy black fossil discs) visible through the open slots, a squat cylindrical hopper canister with a snap-on lid standing beside them holding more discs, small rectangular hand-trays scattered on the table, next to a cardboard game box illustrated with a cross-section of colorful rock strata and fossils, warm earthy studio lighting, isometric product-photography angle.

ideas.title: Signal Fire
ideas.concept: Fixed mountain peaks of different heights sit permanently on the board, and whether your beacon can 'see' another one is decided by physically laying a notched sighting gauge across the terrain between them — no guessing, no dice, just geometry you can check with your hands. Race to relay a chain of beacons from your home valley to the summit before the storm catches you.
ideas.differentiation: An original elevation/line-of-sight race whose defining mechanism is a set of pre-computed physical sighting-gauge templates (one per fixed post-to-post distance) that deterministically resolve whether a sightline is blocked, rather than mental math, a spinner, or dice. Searched 'board game elevation peg height line of sight signal relay beacon mountain' and 'physical sighting gauge template line of sight board game deterministic' — found Santorini (3D elevation building/movement, no sightline-gauge mechanic) and real-world laser-mirror-reflection patents (a different mechanism: beam redirection via rotating mirrors, not fixed-terrain line-of-sight checking); no existing product uses printed notched sighting-gauge templates to resolve line-of-sight on a fixed-elevation board.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players (playable as a pure race, or as a team-vs-storm variant for 2). Setup: place the fixed terrain board on the table (7 permanent raised elevation posts: 1 home valley per player at height 0, shared waypoint peaks at 20/40/60/80mm, and 1 summit post at 100mm, all molded into the one-piece board). Place the storm marker at position 0 on the 24-space ring track around the board. Each player takes 4 beacon base pegs and 12 height collars (3 per peg) in their color. On your turn, do ONE of: (a) Place one beacon peg on any empty post (your home post, a shared waypoint, or the summit if you have an unbroken chain reaching it), choosing 0-3 height collars to stack on it first, limited by your remaining collar supply. (b) Attempt a Signal Check between two of your OWN beacons already on the board: pick the pre-printed sighting gauge labeled for that specific pair of posts (each gauge has a notched profile at the correct blocking height for every intervening post given the board's fixed geometry), lay it flat across the row of posts between your two beacons — if no intervening peg (yours or an opponent's) pokes up higher than the gauge's notch at that post, the sightline is clear: place a connector bead to mark a completed link. After every turn, roll the d6 and advance the storm marker that many spaces. The first player to complete an unbroken chain of connector-linked beacons from home to summit wins immediately. If the storm marker reaches space 24 first, the game ends and whoever has the most connector-linked beacon pairs wins.
ideas.components: 1 terrain board (single-piece printed relief board, ~350x250mm, integrated raised posts at fixed heights 0/20/40/60/80/100mm, textured mountain paint scheme); 16 beacon base pegs (4 per player color, 8mm dia base); 48 height collars (12 per color, 10mm tall snap-on rings, stack up to 3 per peg); 6 sighting template gauges (flat comb-profile rulers, one per distinct post-to-post distance, 5mm thick, notch heights precomputed from the board's fixed geometry); 1 storm marker pawn + printed 24-space ring track; 30 connector beads (8mm, 4 colors); 1 d6; box.
ideas.demand_case: Elevation/verticality as a core mechanic has a validated audience — Santorini ranked among 'the 100 most important games of the 2010s' and remains a widely-stocked title, showing real demand for physical-height-based spatial puzzles. Target audience: family-to-light-hobbyist strategy players, ages 10+, who enjoy tactile geometric puzzles like Santorini or Ricochet Robots.
ideas.fun_case: Because the sighting gauges make blocking fully deterministic and checkable by hand, the core decision each turn is a genuine spatial-planning puzzle rather than a luck check — the same 'read the fixed geometry correctly' satisfaction that makes Santorini's elevation rules engaging, compressed into a ~25-35 minute race under a rising storm clock.
ideas.producibility_notes: 5 part types. The terrain board's integrated posts are single-print geometry apart from the beacon pegs snapping onto them (5mm peg, 0.2mm clearance, repeated 16 times, one uniform validated joint). Height collars use a simple friction snap-ring (8.2mm inner dia over an 8mm peg, 0.2mm clearance) repeated across 48 parts but one geometry. The sighting gauges are flat, jointless parts (a notched profile ruler) — this makes the line-of-sight check fully deterministic from board geometry alone (all heights/distances fixed at design time, notch profile computed directly from that geometry) rather than requiring physical iteration to know if it's fair. No features under 1mm.

ideas.title: Auction House: Curios
ideas.concept: A rotating auction wheel reveals exactly one curio for sale at a time, refilled automatically from a gravity hopper as it turns — and every player's bid tokens, numbered 1 through 10, can each only be spent once for the entire game. Every silent bid is a resource-allocation gamble: burn your 10 now on a lot you might regret, or save it for something better two turns from now that might never come.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: For Sale's spend-a-unique-bid-value-once sealed auction, where several lots are visible simultaneously each round. Rule-level change: Auction House: Curios reveals only one lot at a time through a physically rotating wheel with a gravity-fed hopper auto-refill, removing the ability to compare against other visible lots before bidding and replacing the card-deck lot display with a mechanical rotating/refilling apparatus. Searched 'board game rotating auction wheel bid dial spinner mechanic' and 'gravity hopper auto refill auction wheel single lot reveal board game' — found only generic auction/bidding mechanism overviews and unrelated spinner accessories; no existing shipped product combines a rotating single-lot auction wheel with gravity-hopper refill and unique-value-once bidding.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players. Setup: load the hopper column with the curio chip supply (40 chips, engraved with a hidden value 1-10 on the underside, decorative icon on top, shuffled by hand). Load 8 chips face-up into the 8 pockets of the auction wheel and set the wheel so pocket 1 sits under the fixed pointer. Each player takes a personal set of bid tokens numbered 1-10 (each used once over the whole game) and 40 coin tokens. Each round, all players act: (1) The curio under the pointer is the active lot. Every player secretly selects ONE unused bid token and places it face-down. (2) Reveal simultaneously. Highest bid wins the lot, pays that many coins to the bank, and takes the curio chip, revealing its hidden point value. Both winner's and losers' used bid tokens are set aside, unusable for the rest of the game (losers pay nothing). Ties broken by seating proximity to the pointer. (3) Rotate the wheel one pocket clockwise; the pocket that just passed the reload position (opposite the pointer) automatically drops its next chip from the hopper into the newly empty pocket. Repeat until the hopper is empty and all 8 wheel pockets have been won (40 total lots). Final scoring: sum the hidden point values of curios you won. Most points wins; ties broken by most coins remaining.
ideas.components: 1 auction wheel assembly (printed disc, 8 pockets around the rim, ~250mm diameter, mounted on a center pivot with a fixed pointer arm on the base stand); 1 hopper column (printed vertical chute behind the wheel, gravity-feeds one chip at a time into the reload pocket as the wheel rotates past it, holds up to 32 reserve chips); 40 curio chips (25mm hex, decorative icon top face, engraved value 1-10 on underside); 40 bid tokens (10 numbered chips x 4 colors); 160 coin tokens (denominations 1/5/10, ~40 per player); 1 turn-order/pointer marker; box.
ideas.demand_case: Auction/bidding is a long-standing core BGG mechanism category with proven mainstream sellers — For Sale (Alan R. Moon, in continuous print since 1997) and Ra remain widely stocked gateway-to-mid-weight auction classics, demonstrating durable demand for a unique-value-once bidding structure. Target audience: family-to-light-hobbyist gamers, ages 10+, who enjoy tight bidding/knapsack-style games.
ideas.fun_case: The core tension — burn a high bid now on a so-so lot, or save it and risk rivals scooping the good ones later — is the exact unique-value knapsack bidding decision that makes For Sale replayable; here it's stretched across a slower one-lot-at-a-time reveal, raising the stakes of each individual bid since you can't compare against future lots before deciding. ~30-40 min playtime fits the stated audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: 3 main mechanical parts (wheel, pointer stand, hopper). The gravity hopper feed is the standout custom mechanism — spec the internal chute at chip-thickness-plus-1mm clearance (6mm chute for 5mm chips) with a single-chip-at-a-time baffle step at the reload position; this is a known dispenser-mechanism category (similar to a candy/token dispenser) whose function depends purely on fixed chute geometry and gravity, so it should be validated with one physical print-and-drop-test pass before locking the STL. The wheel's center pivot reuses the same peg+bushing joint validated elsewhere (6mm pin, 0.3mm clearance). No features under 1mm.

ideas.title: Meteor Mining
ideas.concept: Roll five ore dice up to three times per turn, chasing sets and straights to fill the categories on your asteroid claim board — same push-your-luck dice-scoring roots as the classic that made this genre a household staple, just recast as a sci-fi mining operation with reusable peg scorecards instead of paper.
ideas.differentiation: Base game: Yahtzee (Milton Bradley/Hasbro, 1956) — standard 5-dice, 3-rolls-per-turn, 13-category scoring with no rule changes. Styling concept: asteroid-mining sci-fi theme — dice recast as 'ore dice' (same 1-6 pip distribution, restyled as mineral-vein icons), dice cup restyled as a drill-rig hopper, and the paper scoresheet replaced with a reusable engraved pegboard scorecard per player (a necessary printable substitute since paper isn't in scope for a manufactured product). Searched 'Yahtzee sci-fi mining reskin 3D print' and 'asteroid mining dice game pegboard scorecard' — found generic dice games and unrelated mining-themed strategy games (e.g., Drillers) but no existing product combining the exact Yahtzee ruleset with an asteroid-mining reskin and reusable pegboard scorecard.
ideas.rules: 2-6 players. Each player takes a scorecard board with 13 category tracks (Ones, Twos, Threes, Fours, Fives, Sixes, 3-of-a-Kind, 4-of-a-Kind, Full House, Small Straight, Large Straight, Chance, YAHTZEE) plus an Upper Section subtotal track and bonus marker. On your turn, roll all 5 ore dice using the drill-rig hopper cup. You may re-roll any subset of dice up to two more times (3 rolls total per turn), setting aside dice you want to keep between rolls. After your final roll, choose exactly one unfilled category to score: place your peg at the position matching your dice result under standard Yahtzee scoring (Ones-Sixes = sum of matching dice; 3/4-of-a-Kind = sum of all 5 dice if you have 3+/4+ matching, else 0; Full House = 25; Small Straight = 30; Large Straight = 40; Chance = sum of all 5 dice; YAHTZEE = 50, with each additional Yahtzee after your first scored one worth a 100-point bonus peg). Every category can only be pegged once per player; if you cannot or do not want to score in any open category with your roll, you must peg a zero in one open category. If your Ones-Sixes pegs sum to 63 or more, move your bonus marker to add 35 bonus points. The game ends when every player has filled all 13 categories. Highest total score wins.
ideas.components: 5 ore dice (16mm, standard pip layout restyled as mineral-vein icon counts 1-6); 1 drill-rig hopper dice cup (printed conical cup with a textured rim); 6 pegboard scorecards (13 category tracks each with a numbered peg-hole row, an upper-section subtotal track, and a bonus-Yahtzee peg track); 78 score pegs (13 per player, small colored pegs, removable/reusable for replay); box.
ideas.demand_case: Yahtzee is one of the best-selling dice games of all time, with Hasbro citing it as a perennial top-seller across decades, and roll-and-score push-your-luck remains one of the largest casual-game audiences on BGG. Target audience: broad family/casual game night, ages 6+.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision — bank a mediocre category now versus risk a re-roll chasing a rare Yahtzee — is proven across decades of play to be replayable and accessible; the reskin changes nothing about that proven decision structure, only the tactile/thematic presentation, while the reusable pegboard scorecard removes the paper-scoresheet friction of the original.
ideas.producibility_notes: 4 part types, all simple. Pegboard scorecard has 13 rows x up to 63 peg-hole positions each — many repeated small holes (5mm dia, 0.2mm clearance) but one validated hole geometry repeated many times, not a novel mechanism. No features under 1mm on the dice (pip/icon depressions kept at 1.5mm minimum for print fidelity). No joints beyond simple peg-in-hole.

ideas.title: Neon Skyline
ideas.concept: A double-six domino set restyled as glowing skyscraper silhouettes against a night sky — match building notch counts end-to-end exactly as you would pips, racing to be first to place your whole skyline or lock the game when no one can move.
ideas.differentiation: Base game: standard double-six dominoes (28-tile set, traditional block/draw rules, no rule changes). Styling concept: nighttime city-skyline theme — each domino end shows a raised notch count (0-6) styled as illuminated windows on a stacked skyscraper silhouette instead of dots, tile bodies textured/colored as dark building facades. Searched 'dominoes skyscraper skyline reskin 3D print' and 'neon city dominoes board game' — found generic domino sets and unrelated city-building tile games but no existing product combining a standard double-six domino ruleset with a skyscraper-silhouette notch-matching restyle.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players. Shuffle all 28 domino tiles face-down and each player draws 7 (2-player) or 5 (3-4 player); remaining tiles form the draw boneyard. The player with the highest double (or highest total notch-count if none drawn) plays first by placing that tile in the center. Play proceeds clockwise: on your turn, place one tile from your hand with a matching notch-count end touching an open end already on the layout. If you have no legal play, draw from the boneyard one tile at a time until you can play or the boneyard is empty (then pass). A double tile is placed perpendicular across the line and opens two new ends at right angles to future play. Round ends when a player plays their last tile ('Skyline!') or when no player can play and the boneyard is empty (blocked game). Scoring: the round winner scores the sum of all notch-counts remaining in every other player's hand; in a blocked game, each player scores the difference between their own remaining hand total and the lowest hand total among players not already at 0. Play multiple rounds; first player to reach 100 points wins the game.
ideas.components: 28 domino tiles (double-six set, each ~50x25x8mm, dark charcoal PLA with raised notch-pip counts styled as lit windows, subtle color accent trim per tile); 1 domino tray/rack insert to hold a hand of tiles on edge; 1 score track board (0-100 track) with 4 slide markers; box.
ideas.demand_case: Dominoes is one of the most enduringly popular tile games worldwide, with the classic double-six set remaining a top-selling evergreen game category across mass retailers, and neon-cyberpunk night-city aesthetics are a proven strong-selling styling direction for premium reskin editions of classic games. Target audience: broad family/casual game night, ages 6+, plus a style-conscious buyer wanting a striking tabletop-display object.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision — hold your doubles for tempo, block opponents' open ends, manage which numbers you're hoarding — is the same well-proven tension that's kept dominoes played worldwide for centuries; the reskin changes nothing structurally, so the fun case rests entirely on the proven base game plus the added tactile/display appeal of a stylized 3D-printed skyline set.
ideas.producibility_notes: 3 part types, minimal risk. Domino tiles are solid blocks with shallow embossed/debossed notch details (spec notch depressions at 1.2mm depth minimum for crisp visibility, avoiding sub-1mm fine detail). Tray insert is a simple open-slot rack, no joints. Score track uses the same slide-marker groove geometry validated elsewhere (0.3mm groove clearance). No electronics, no fragile parts.
